bib.title: Memory-R1: Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Memory-R1: Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning". Sikuan Yan*, Xiufeng Yang*, Zuchao Huang, Ercong Nie, Zifeng Ding, Zonggen Li, Xiaowen Ma, Jinhe Bi, Kristian Kersting, Jeff Z. Pan, Hinrich Schuetze, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma (corresponding author). Affiliations: LMU Munich and Munich Center for Machine Learning (lead), TU Munich, Cambridge, HKU, TU Darmstadt, Edinburgh. Venue: preprint, arXiv:2508.19828v5 [cs.CL], 14 Jan 2026. The text gives no venue, though the format looks like an ACL template. 2025 per the filename and arXiv ID.

COVERAGE: All 20 of 20 pages, 72,349 of 72,349 chars, including limitations, appendices A to G, tables 1 to 5 and the algorithms. I skimmed the references. Figure 3 to 8 and 13 to 14 data are plots, so their numbers are not in the extraction. I did not run the figures script.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Memory-R1-GRPO beats the strongest baseline, MemoryOS, on LoCoMo with LLaMA-3.1-8B. This is a relative gain, not absolute.
  number: Overall F1 45.02, B1 37.51, J 62.74 (Table 1) vs MemoryOS 35.04 / 27.99 / 48.20. Relative gains are 28.5%, 34.0% and 30.2%. PPO gains are 17.2%, 17.6% and 19.4%.
  setup: LoCoMo, adversarial subset excluded, 1307 test questions, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, temperature 0, baselines re-implemented by the authors.
  quote: "Memory-R1-GRPO delivers the strongest overall performance, improving F1 by 28.5%, B1 by 34.0%, and J by 30.2% relatively over the strongest baseline MemoryOS."
  where: p.6, section 4.2; Table 1, p.6
- The intro and abstract name Mem0 as the baseline for the same gains, which contradicts section 4.2.
  quote: "Memory-R1 delivers substantial gains over the most competitive baseline, Mem0"
  where: p.2. Table 1 shows Mem0 at 30.41 F1, so MemoryOS is the stronger baseline. Cite section 4.2, not the intro.
- Training is very cheap in labels. Only 152 QA pairs are used, with no operation labels.
  number: 152 train / 81 validation / 1307 test (1:1:8 split).
  quote: "we exclude the adversarial subset and use a 1:1:8 train/validation/test split (152/81/1307 questions)."
  where: p.5, 4.1
- RL beats supervised imitation of a stronger teacher. Memory-SFT is behaviour cloning from GPT-5 trajectories on the same data and architecture.
  number: LLaMA overall J is SFT 58.76 vs GRPO 62.74 and PPO 57.54. F1 is SFT 42.81 vs GRPO 45.02 and PPO 41.05. Qwen-7B J is SFT 61.13 vs GRPO 61.51, a near tie.
  quote: "Notably, while Memory-SFT benefits from guidance by a powerful teacher model (GPT-5), our reinforcement learning approach still outperforms it"
  where: p.6; Table 1. The margin is small. PPO on LLaMA is below SFT on J, and the paper reports no seeds or variance.
- Memory Manager reward is outcome-only. It scores downstream answer exact match through a frozen Answer Agent, so no operation labels are needed.
  quote: "R_answer = EM(y_pred, y_gold)" and "This exact-match signal requires no manual labels, remains scalable, and is sufficient to teach effective memory operations."
  where: p.4, section 3.1
- The learned manager is worth about 6 to 8 points.
  number: Without the RL Manager under PPO, F1/B1/J fall from 41.0/32.9/57.5 to 34.5/28.1/49.0. Under GRPO the figure is 37.5/30.6/52.9 (full pipeline 45.0/37.5/62.7).
  setup: LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.
  quote: "Under PPO, F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-as-a-Judge drop from 41.0, 32.9, and 57.5 to 34.5, 28.1, and 49.0, respectively."
  where: p.7, 4.4
- Memory distillation (the Answer Agent selects relevant entries out of 60 retrieved) helps, especially under GRPO.
  number: PPO 39.3/30.9/57.4 to 41.0/32.9/57.5. GRPO 41.0/34.4/60.1 to 45.0/37.5/62.7.
  quote: "GRPO shows larger gains, increasing from 41.0, 34.4, and 60.1 to 45.0, 37.5, and 62.7."
  where: p.7. 60 = 30 memories per speaker (Algorithm 2, p.15).
- Answer Agent gains compound with manager quality.
  number: Gains with a LLaMA-3.1-8B manager vs a GPT-4o-mini manager. F1 +10.10 vs +19.72, B1 +10.81 vs +18.19, J +5.05 vs +15.76.
  quote: "Improvements are larger with the stronger manager (F1: +10.10 vs. +19.72; BLEU-1: +10.81 vs. +18.19; J: +5.05 vs. +15.76)"
  where: p.7
- Zero-shot transfer. Training is on LoCoMo only. On LongMemEval, GRPO scores best in Table 5.
  number: LLaMA overall F1/B1/J is 45.20/39.30/55.40 for GRPO vs A-Mem 38.36/33.30/54.20. Qwen-7B is 46.70/41.10/57.80 for GRPO vs A-Mem 41.55/36.58/54.80, with PPO at 47.40 J. On LLaMA, GRPO's J lead over A-Mem is only 1.2 points and over Memory-SFT 0.6. On Qwen, PPO's overall F1 (40.30) is below the A-Mem and Memory-SFT scores. MSC results are only in Figure 4.
  quote: "Memory-R1-GRPO outperforms all baseline systems across both LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B backbones."
  where: p.17, Table 5
- Scale: gains hold at 3B, 7B and 14B (Qwen-2.5). Table 3 gives base-to-GRPO figures.
  number: Overall J is 41.24 to 57.92 (3B), 58.38 to 57.46 (7B, a drop), and 50.80 to 63.50 (14B). Overall F1 is 24.18 to 40.45 (3B), 29.36 to 41.31 (7B) and 36.91 to 44.40 (14B).
  quote: "Memory-R1 consistently outperforms the base model at every scale"
  where: p.6; Table 3, p.18. The "every scale" claim does not hold for J at 7B GRPO (58.38 base vs 57.46).
- Reward design matters. A J-based reward yields verbose answers, so the authors use EM.
  number: PPO with J reward: F1 33.69, B1 23.36, J 63.58. PPO with EM reward: 41.05 / 32.91 / 57.54.
  quote: "PPO with J-based reward achieves higher J scores but lower F1 and B1 due to verbose outputs"
  where: p.8, Table 2
- Learned distillation beats a reranker on accuracy and latency. Figure 8 is a plot only.
  quote: "While reranking provides modest accuracy gains, it incurs substantial latency overhead."
  where: p.8
- Latency. The GRPO Answer Agent is faster than base and PPO.
  number: LLaMA p50/p95 is 0.34/0.67 s for GRPO vs 0.65/3.07 s for base and 0.91/4.67 s for PPO. Manager p50 is about 2 s (1.98 to 2.17 s) with p95 about 3.4 to 3.6 s. Search p50 is under 0.35 s.
  quote: "the GRPO-trained Answer Agent achieves substantially lower median and tail latency, with p50 and p95 of 0.34 s and 0.67 s, compared to 0.65 s and 3.07 s for the base model and 0.91 s and 4.67 s for PPO."
  where: p.19, App. G
- A vanilla in-context manager fragments memory. Given "adopted Buddy" and then "adopted Scout", it issues DELETE+ADD, while the RL manager issues one UPDATE. This is anecdotal, from two cases.
  quote: "A vanilla system misinterprets this as a contradiction, issuing DELETE+ADD and overwriting the original memory."
  where: p.2 and App. A.1
- PPO vs GRPO training. GRPO converges faster early (Figure 7), and both reach similar final reward.
  quote: "both methods steadily improve and ultimately reach comparable final reward levels."
  where: p.8

LIMITS
- Authors concede the evaluation is dialogue-only and multimodal is untested. They train the Manager and Answer Agent separately (the other is frozen) because rewards are sparse, and call end-to-end multi-agent RL future work. (p.9)
- Not shown: variance or seeds, any test of memory-bank growth over very long horizons, and cost of training beyond the hardware given.
- Baselines are re-implemented by the authors at temperature 0 with a 2048 token cap. Results may differ from published numbers.
- The LLM-as-a-judge is lenient by design ("be generous with your grading"), and the judge model is not named in the main text.
- Training data builds the memory bank with GPT-4o-mini. Memory-SFT uses GPT-5 trajectories, so the pipeline is not teacher-free.
- Internal inconsistency: the temporal memory bank is built from the previous 24 turns (App. B.2 text) vs 50 turns (Algorithm 1).
- The text says the Answer Agent is trained after the Manager. The ablation "without RL Answer Agent" J values (59.4, 59.9) exceed the full-pipeline PPO J (57.5), so J does not always improve.

BUILDS ON
- Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025): the {ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, NOOP} operator set, prompts and top-60 retrieval.
- MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023): MSC setup and memory buffers.
- LoCoMo (Maharana et al. 2024) and LongMemEval (Wu et al. 2024).
- PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) and GRPO (Shao et al. 2024), run in the VERL framework (Sheng et al. 2025).
- Search-R1 (Jin et al. 2025): outcome-reward RL for tool use.
- Baselines: A-Mem (Xu et al. 2025), MemoryOS (Kang et al. 2025).
- Others cited: Tensor Brain (Tresp et al. 2023), the AIOS memory API.

CODE (prompts and algorithms, verbatim)
- GRPO advantage: `A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r)` (Eq. 3, p.4).
- Manager policy: `(o, m') ~ π_θ(· | x, M_old)` (Eq. 1, p.4).
- Manager prompt events are `"event" : "ADD" | "UPDATE" | "DELETE" | "NONE"`, and updates keep the same ID and an `old_memory` field (Figs 9 and 10, pp.14 to 15).
- Answer Agent prompt rules: "IMPORTANT: Select memories you found that are useful for answering the questions, and output it before you answer questions." and "The answer should be less than 5-6 words." (Fig 11, p.16).
- Hyperparameters (p.15): 4 H100s (8 for 14B), batch 128, micro-batch 2, max prompt/response 4096/2048 tokens. PPO actor/critic learning rates 1e-6 and 1e-5. Training temperature 1.0, evaluation temperature 0.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): vanilla DELETE+ADD vs RL UPDATE, with 60 memories distilled to one. Fastest explanation of the point.
- Fig 2 (p.4): two-stage pipeline (Memory Manager, then Answer Agent with distillation).
- Fig 3 (p.6): scaling across Qwen 3B, 7B and 14B.
- Fig 4 (p.6): zero-shot transfer to MSC and LongMemEval.
- Fig 5 (p.7): ablations.
- Fig 6 (p.8): manager-quality compounding.
- Fig 7 (p.8): PPO vs GRPO reward curves.
- Fig 8 (p.8): accuracy and latency against a reranker.
- Figs 13 and 14 (p.20): latency against accuracy by component.
Captions come from the extraction text only.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Table cell layout is partly garbled where bold values merge with neighbours (for example "54.65 42.81", "50.63 26.57"). Numbers quoted above were checked against context, but Table 3 and 4 bolding is unreliable.
- Figure data is not extractable as text, so Fig 3 to 8 values are unread.
- Intro vs section 4.2 baseline naming conflict and the 24 vs 50 turn conflict (see LIMITS).
